source_text: Πλὴν καὶ ἄκων ἐνέπεσεν ὁ Κέλσος εἰς τὸ μαρτυρεῖν τῷ νεώτερον εἶναι τὸν κόσμον καὶ οὐδέπω μυρίων ἐτῶν εἰπὼν καὶ Ἕλληνας ταῦτα νομίζειν ἀρχαῖα, ὡς πρεσβύτερα διὰ τοὺς κατακλυσμοὺς καὶ τὰς ἐκπυρώσεις οὐ τεθεωρήκασιν οὐδ᾿ ἀπομνημονεύουσιν. ἔστωσαν δὲ τῷ Κέλσῳ τοῦ περὶ τῶν ἐκπυρώσεων καὶ ἐξυδατώσεων μύθου διδάσκαλοι οἱ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν σοφώτατοι Αἰγύπτιοι, ὧν τῆς σοφίας ἴχνη ἄλογα ζῷα προσκυνούμενα καὶ λόγοι παριστάντες εὔλογον εἶναι καὶ ἀνακεχωρηκυῖάν τινα καὶ μυστικὴν τὴν τοιαύτην τοῦ θεοῦ θεραπείαν. κἂν μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι περὶ τῶν ζῴων σεμνύνοντες ἑαυτῶν τὸν λόγον θεολογίας φέρωσι, σοφοί εἰσιν· ἐὰν δὲ ὁ τῷ Ἰουδαίων συγκαταθέμενος νόμῳ καὶ νομοθέτῃ πάντα ἀναφέρῃ ἐπὶ τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργὸν μόνον θεὸν. ἥττων εἶναι παρὰ Κέλσῳ καὶ τοῖς ὁμοίοις αὐτῷ λογίζεται τοῦ μὴ εἰς λογικὰ μόνον καὶ θνητὰ ζῷα ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς ἄλογα κατάγοντος τὴν θεότητα ὑπὲρ τὴν μυθικὴν μετενσωμάτωσιν. τὴν περὶ τῆς πιπτούσης ἀπὸ τῶν ἁψίδων τοῦ οὐρανοῦ ψυχῆς καὶ ἕως τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων, οὐ μόνον ἡμέρων ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀγριωτάτων. καταβαινούσης. καὶ ἐὰν μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι μυθολογῶσι, πιστεύονται πεφιλοσοφηκέναι δι᾿ αἰνιγμῶν καὶ ἀποῤῥήτων, ἐὰν δὲ Μω(??)σῆς ὅλῳ ἔθνει συγγράφων ἱστορίας καὶ νόμους αὐτοῖς καταλίπῃ. μῦθοι κενοὶ νομίζονται μηδ᾿ ἀλληγορίαν ἐπιδεχόμενοι οἱ λόγοι αὐτοῦ·
thought_title: Celsus' Views on the World and Divinity
pass_a_gloss: But also Celsus unwillingly fell into testifying that the world is younger and not yet ten thousand years old, having said that Greeks also think these things are ancient, as they have not observed nor remembered older things because of the floods and conflagrations. Let the most wise Egyptians, according to him, be the teachers of the myth about conflagrations and inundations, whose wisdom is indicated by irrational animals being worshiped and words presenting a logical argument and having retreated to some mystical divine service. And if Egyptians, honoring animals, bring their argument to a theological level, they are wise; but if the one who lays down the law with the Jews and the lawgiver refers everything to the one God, the creator of all. It is considered by Celsus and those like him to be inferior, the one who does not lead divinity only to rational and mortal animals but also to irrational animals, beyond the mythical transmigration. The thing about the soul falling from the vaults of heaven, even to irrational animals, not only tame but also wild, descending. And if Egyptians mythologize, they are believed to have philosophized through riddles and arcane sayings; but if Moses, writing history and laws for the whole nation, leaves them behind, his words are considered empty myths, not admitting allegory.
pass_b_english: Celsus unintentionally testified that the world is relatively young, with an age of less than ten thousand years, a view also shared by the Greeks, who consider these events ancient because they have no record or memory of anything older due to floods and conflagrations (no specific reference). The Egyptians, according to Celsus, are the authorities on the myth of conflagrations and inundations, and their wisdom is reflected in the worship of irrational animals and the presentation of logical arguments, which they believe is a form of mystical divine service. If the Egyptians' reverence for animals is rooted in a theological perspective, then they can be considered wise. However, if the lawgiver, who is in agreement with the Jews, attributes everything to the one God, the creator of all, then this perspective is viewed as inferior by Celsus and like-minded individuals, who believe that divinity should only be associated with rational and mortal beings, not irrational animals, which they see as a form of mythical transmigration. This idea of the soul descending from the heavens to irrational animals, whether tame or wild, is also part of this belief system. While the Egyptians' use of mythology may be seen as a form of philosophical expression, using riddles and arcane sayings to convey their message, the writings of Moses, which include history and laws for the entire nation, are dismissed as empty myths that do not allow for allegorical interpretation. The notion that the soul can fall from the vaults of heaven to even the most irrational of animals is a concept that is deeply ingrained in this worldview, and it is this idea that Celsus and those who think like him find to be lacking in substance.

review.notes: Pass B adds significant content and interpretive commentary not present in the Greek source, specifically the concluding sentence: 'The notion that the soul can fall from the vaults of heaven to even the most irrational of animals is a concept that is deeply ingrained in this worldview, and it is this idea that Celsus and those who think like him find to be lacking in substance.' This is an expansion/paraphrase rather than a translation. Additionally, Pass B includes a parenthetical '(no specific reference)' which is not in the source. Pass A is a more faithful translation but the presence of the additive content in Pass B violates the rule that Pass B must neither add to nor contradict A or the Greek.
uncertainties: The Greek text contains an uncertain reading 'Μω(??)σῆς'.
reasons: Pass B adds an entire concluding sentence of interpretation: 'The notion that the soul can fall from the vaults of heaven to even the most irrational of animals is a concept that is deeply ingrained in this worldview, and it is this idea that Celsus and those who think like him find to be lacking in substance.'

The Pass A translation omits the phrase 'κἂν μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι μυθολογῶσι, πιστεύονται πεφιλοσοφηκέναι δι᾿ αἰνιγμῶν καὶ ἀποῤῥήτων, ἐὰν δὲ Μω(??)σῆς ὅλῳ ἔθνει συγγράφων ἱστορίας καὶ νόμους αὐτοῖς καταλίπῃ.' (Pass A omits this entire section).

The Pass A translation incorrectly states 'the Greeks also think these things are ancient' when the Greek says 'Ἕλληνας ταῦτα νομίζειν ἀρχαῖα' which means 'the Greeks consider these things to be ancient.'

The Pass A translation misrepresents the phrase 'πιστεύονται πεφιλοσοφηκέναι δι᾿ αἰνιγμῶν καὶ ἀποῤῥήτων' as 'they are believed to have philosophized through riddles and arcane sayings,' which is a misinterpretation of the original Greek.
